claim: In symptomatic SOD1G93A mice, ephrinB2 expression was dramatically increased in ventral horn astrocytes.
source: In symptomatic SOD1G93A mice (a well-established ALS model), ephrinB2 expression was dramatically increased in ventral horn astrocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing ephrinB2 upregulation in the ventral horn of SOD1G93A mice at symptomatic stages, as presented in the abstract and detailed in the results section with quantitative measurements.

claim: Reducing ephrinB2 in the cervical spinal cord ventral horn via viral-mediated shRNA delivery reduced motor neuron loss in SOD1G93A mice.
source: Reducing ephrinB2 in the cervical spinal cord ventral horn via viral-mediated shRNA delivery reduced motor neuron loss and preserved respiratory function by maintaining phrenic motor neuron innervation of diaphragm.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased motor neuron counts in the cervical spinal cord of SOD1G93A mice treated with lenti-shRNA-Efnb2 compared to controls, as shown in Figure 3 and described in the results.

claim: Reducing ephrinB2 in the cervical spinal cord ventral horn preserved respiratory function by maintaining phrenic motor neuron innervation of diaphragm in SOD1G93A mice.
source: Reducing ephrinB2 in the cervical spinal cord ventral horn via viral-mediated shRNA delivery reduced motor neuron loss and preserved respiratory function by maintaining phrenic motor neuron innervation of diaphragm.
evidence: This claim is supported by CMAP recordings showing larger amplitudes in shRNA-treated animals and morphological analysis showing increased fully-innervated NMJs in the diaphragm.

claim: EphrinB2 expression was elevated in human ALS spinal cord.
source: EphrinB2 expression was also elevated in human ALS spinal cord.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting analysis on postmortem samples from human ALS donors with SOD1 mutations showing increased ephrinB2 protein expression compared to non-diseased controls, as shown in Figure 6.

claim: ALS is characterized by loss of upper motor neurons in the brain and lower motor neurons of spinal cord and brainstem.
source: In ALS, loss of upper motor neurons (MNs) in the brain and lower MNs of spinal cord and brainstem results in progressive muscle paralysis and ultimately in death, usually in only 2–5 years after diagnosis (Bruijn et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature on ALS pathology.

claim: ALS results in progressive muscle paralysis and death, usually in only 2-5 years after diagnosis.
source: In ALS, loss of upper motor neurons (MNs) in the brain and lower MNs of spinal cord and brainstem results in progressive muscle paralysis and ultimately in death, usually in only 2–5 years after diagnosis (Bruijn et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature on ALS disease progression.

claim: The majority of ALS cases are sporadic, while 10% are of the familial form.
source: The majority of ALS cases are sporadic, while 10% are of the familial form; these familial cases are linked to a variety of genes such as Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1; Rosen, 1993), TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) (Mackenzie et al., 2007), C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011; Renton et al., 2011) and others.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on ALS epidemiology and genetics.

claim: Familial ALS cases are linked to genes including SOD1, TDP-43, and C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion.
source: The majority of ALS cases are sporadic, while 10% are of the familial form; these familial cases are linked to a variety of genes such as Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1; Rosen, 1993), TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) (Mackenzie et al., 2007), C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011; Renton et al., 2011) and others.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature identifying specific genes associated with familial ALS.

claim: Non-neuronal cell types such as astrocytes play significant roles in ALS pathogenesis.
source: In particular, non-neuronal cell types such as astrocytes play significant roles in disease pathogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by the broader context of the manuscript and citations to literature on astrocyte involvement in ALS.

claim: Transcellular signaling between astrocytes and motor neurons may represent an important regulatory node for motor neuron survival and disease progression in ALS.
source: Findings suggest that transcellular signaling between astrocytes and MNs may represent an important regulatory node for MN survival and disease progression in ALS (Yamanaka and Komine, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on astrocyte-motor neuron interactions in ALS.

claim: Ephs are transmembrane signaling molecules and the largest known family of receptor tyrosine kinases in the mammalian genome.
source: Ephs are transmembrane signaling molecules and the largest known family of receptor tyrosine kinases in the mammalian genome.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Eph receptors in the scientific literature.

claim: Ephs bind to and are activated by ephrins, which are either glycosylphosphatidylinositol-linked (ephrin-As) or transmembrane proteins (ephrin-Bs) also capable of signaling.
source: Ephs bind to and are activated by ephrins, which are either glycosylphosphatidylinositol-linked (ephrin-As) or are transmembrane proteins (ephrin-Bs) also capable of signaling (Klein, 2009; Pasquale, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on Eph-ephrin signaling mechanisms.

claim: Eph-ephrin transcellular signaling regulates dendritic spine formation, dendritic filopodia-dependent synaptogenesis, axon guidance, control of synapse maintenance and density, and synaptic localization of glutamate receptor subunits.
source: Eph-ephrin transcellular signaling regulates many events in the developing and mature nervous system that are mediated by cell contact dependent mechanisms, including: dendritic spine formation, dendritic filopodia-dependent synaptogenesis, axon guidance, control of synapse maintenance and density, and synaptic localization of glutamate receptor subunits (Klein, 2009; Pasquale, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on Eph-ephrin signaling functions.

claim: Neuronal EphA binding to glial ephrin plays an important role in the morphogenesis of dendritic spines.
source: Neuronal EphA binding to glial ephrin plays an important role in the morphogenesis of dendritic spines (Murai et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on EphA-ephrin interactions in dendritic spine development.

claim: During development, EphA4 is expressed by motor neurons undergoing programmed cell death.
source: Moreover, during development EphA4 is expressed by MNs undergoing programed cell death (Ohta et al., 1996), while blockade of EphA4 signaling can limit cell death in models of stroke (Kandouz, 2018; Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on EphA4 expression during motor neuron development.

claim: Blockade of EphA4 signaling can limit cell death in models of stroke.
source: Moreover, during development EphA4 is expressed by MNs undergoing programed cell death (Ohta et al., 1996), while blockade of EphA4 signaling can limit cell death in models of stroke (Kandouz, 2018; Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on EphA4 signaling in stroke models.

claim: Expression of EphA4 in motor neurons significantly contributes to motor neuron degeneration and overall disease pathogenesis in both rodent and zebrafish animal models of ALS.
source: Expression of EphA4 in MNs significantly contributes to MN degeneration and overall disease pathogenesis in both rodent and zebrafish animal models of ALS (Van Hoecke et al., 2012), while reduction of ephrinA5 worsens disease outcome in an ALS mouse model (Rué et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on EphA4's role in ALS animal models.

claim: Reduction of ephrinA5 worsens disease outcome in an ALS mouse model.
source: Expression of EphA4 in MNs significantly contributes to MN degeneration and overall disease pathogenesis in both rodent and zebrafish animal models of ALS (Van Hoecke et al., 2012), while reduction of ephrinA5 worsens disease outcome in an ALS mouse model (Rué et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on ephrinA5 in ALS models.

claim: Increased EphA4 expression levels and EphA4 signaling capacity correlate with the degree of human ALS disease severity.
source: Furthermore, increased EphA4 expression levels and EphA4 signaling capacity correlate with the degree of human ALS disease severity (Van Hoecke et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on EphA4 in human ALS.

claim: Antisense oligonucleotide or ubiquitous genetic knockdown of EphA4 in ALS mouse models does not affect disease phenotype.
source: While antisense oligonucleotide (Ling et al., 2018) or ubiquitous genetic knockdown (Rué et al., 2019b) of EphA4 in ALS mouse models does not affect disease phenotype, inhibition of EphA4 signaling using EphA4-Fc partially preserves motor function and MN-specific genetic knockdown delays symptomatic onset and protect MNs in ALS mice (Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on EphA4 knockdown studies in ALS models.

claim: Inhibition of EphA4 signaling using EphA4-Fc partially preserves motor function in ALS mice.
source: While antisense oligonucleotide (Ling et al., 2018) or ubiquitous genetic knockdown (Rué et al., 2019b) of EphA4 in ALS mouse models does not affect disease phenotype, inhibition of EphA4 signaling using EphA4-Fc partially preserves motor function and MN-specific genetic knockdown delays symptomatic onset and protect MNs in ALS mice (Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on EphA4-Fc treatment in ALS models.

claim: Motor neuron-specific genetic knockdown of EphA4 delays symptomatic onset and protects motor neurons in ALS mice.
source: While antisense oligonucleotide (Ling et al., 2018) or ubiquitous genetic knockdown (Rué et al., 2019b) of EphA4 in ALS mouse models does not affect disease phenotype, inhibition of EphA4 signaling using EphA4-Fc partially preserves motor function and MN-specific genetic knockdown delays symptomatic onset and protect MNs in ALS mice (Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on motor neuron-specific EphA4 knockdown in ALS models.

claim: In age-matched wild-type littermates, ephrinB2 was expressed at relatively low levels in the cervical ventral horn.
source: In age-matched wild-type (WT) littermates, ephrinB2 was expressed at relatively low levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1a and quantified in Figure 1e.

claim: There was pronounced up-regulation of ephrinB2 in ventral horn at the late pre-symptomatic (60 day) time point in SOD1G93A mice compared to WT controls.
source: Compared to WT controls (Figure 1a), there was pronounced up-regulation of ephrinB2 in ventral horn even at the late pre-symptomatic (60 day) time point (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1b and quantified in Figure 1e showing an 18.58±8.42 fold increase at 60 days.

claim: EphrinB2 expression dramatically increased over disease course in SOD1G93A mice as seen at the symptomatic (120 day) time point.
source: EphrinB2 expression dramatically increased over disease course in SOD1G93A mice as seen at the symptomatic (120 day) time point (Figure 1c) and at disease endstage (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1c and quantified in Figure 1e showing a 41.83±26.67 fold increase at 120 days.

claim: EphrinB2 expression dramatically increased at disease endstage in SOD1G93A mice.
source: EphrinB2 expression dramatically increased over disease course in SOD1G93A mice as seen at the symptomatic (120 day) time point (Figure 1c) and at disease endstage (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1d and quantified in Figure 1e showing a 63.42±10.99 fold increase at endstage.

claim: Compared to WT control, ephrinB2 expression was significantly increased at endstage in the thoracic ventral horn of SOD1G93A mice.
source: Compared to WT control, ephrinB2 expression was also significantly increased at endstage in the thoracic (Figure 1f, g) and lumbar (Figure 1h–k) ventral horn.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1f-g.

claim: Compared to WT control, ephrinB2 expression was significantly increased at endstage in the lumbar ventral horn of SOD1G93A mice.
source: Compared to WT control, ephrinB2 expression was also significantly increased at endstage in the thoracic (Figure 1f, g) and lumbar (Figure 1h–k) ventral horn.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1h-k.

claim: Increases in ephrinB2 expression were localized to spinal cord gray matter.
source: Increases in ephrinB2 expression were localized to spinal cord gray matter.
evidence: This claim is supported by the immunohistochemistry images shown in Figure 1 showing ephrinB2 expression primarily in the gray matter regions.

claim: The vast majority of ephrinB2-expressing cells within the ventral horn displayed an astrocyte-like morphology.
source: Higher magnification imaging from lumbar spinal cord revealed that the vast majority of ephrinB2-expressing cells within the ventral horn displayed an astrocyte-like morphology (Figure 1j, k).
evidence: This claim is supported by high magnification immunohistochemistry images shown in Figure 1j-k.

claim: EphrinB2 upregulation was localized to GFAP-expressing astrocytes in the ventral horn at disease endstage.
source: EphrinB2 upregulation was localized to GFAP-expressing astrocytes (Figure 1o–q) and was not co-localized to NeuN-expressing neurons (Figure 1l–n; n=3 mice).
evidence: This claim is supported by double immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1o-q demonstrating co-localization of ephrinB2 with GFAP.

claim: EphrinB2 was not co-localized to NeuN-expressing neurons in the ventral horn at disease endstage.
source: EphrinB2 upregulation was localized to GFAP-expressing astrocytes (Figure 1o–q) and was not co-localized to NeuN-expressing neurons (Figure 1l–n; n=3 mice).
evidence: This claim is supported by double immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1l-n demonstrating lack of co-localization of ephrinB2 with NeuN.

claim: The majority of GFP-expressing cells in ventral horn following lentiviral injection were GFAP+ reactive astrocytes.
source: The majority of GFP-expressing cells in ventral horn were GFAP+ reactive astrocytes; these GFAP+/GFP+ astrocytes also expressed high levels of ephrinB2, demonstrating that the lentiviral constructs targeted reactive astrocytes that included those with upregulated ephrinB2 expression (Figure 2j–l).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2j-l and quantified in Figure 2m showing 56.53±5.30% of GFP+ cells were GFAP+.

claim: There was little-to-no co-labeling of the GFP reporter with NeuN+ neurons following lentiviral injection.
source: On the contrary, there was little-to-no co-labeling of the GFP reporter with NeuN+ neurons (Figure 2d–f) or cells positive for oligodendrocyte transcription factor 2 (Olig2) (Figure 2g–i), demonstrating that the injected viral constructs did not target a large portion of neurons or cells of the oligodendrocyte lineage within the ventral horn.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2d-f and quantified in Figure 2m showing only 3.54±1.09% of GFP+ cells were NeuN+.

claim: There was little-to-no co-labeling of the GFP reporter with Olig2+ cells following lentiviral injection.
source: On the contrary, there was little-to-no co-labeling of the GFP reporter with NeuN+ neurons (Figure 2d–f) or cells positive for oligodendrocyte transcription factor 2 (Olig2) (Figure 2g–i), demonstrating that the injected viral constructs did not target a large portion of neurons or cells of the oligodendrocyte lineage within the ventral horn.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2g-i and quantified in Figure 2m showing only 0.18±0.18% of GFP+ cells were Olig2+.

claim: The lenti-shRNA vector reduced ephrinB2 expression by approximately a factor of 5 compared to lenti-GFP control.
source: Compared to lenti-GFP control (Figure 2o–q), the lenti-shRNA (Figure 2p–r) reduced ephrinB2 expression by approximately a factor of 5 (Lenti-GFP: 86.92±22.35 GFP+/ephrinB2+ cells, n=3 mice; Lenti-shRNA: 16.67±1.76 GFP+/ephrinB2+ cells, n=3 mice mice; t-test, p=0.035; Figure 2n).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of ephrinB2+/GFP+ cells shown in Figure 2n-r.

claim: Following transduction of Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2, there was a significantly greater number of motor neurons within the ventral horn compared to Lenti-GFP controls in C3-C5 spinal cord.
source: In C3, C4, and C5 following transduction of Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2 (Figure 3d), there was a significantly greater number of MNs within the ventral horn compared to Lenti-GFP controls (Figure 3c) (Lenti-GFP: 266.4±19.46 MNs/µm2, n=4 mice; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2: 344.3±6.31 MNs/µm2, n=4 mice; p=0.019, t-test) (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by motor neuron counts from cresyl violet stained sections shown in Figure 3a-d and quantified in Figure 3b.

claim: Quantification of CMAP amplitude showed a 61% larger amplitude for the lenti-shRNA group compared to lenti-GFP.
source: Quantification of CMAP amplitude showed a 61% larger amplitude for the lenti-shRNA group (Figure 3f) compared to lenti-GFP (Figure 3e–g), demonstrating that ephrinB2 knockdown in cervical ventral horn resulted in significant preservation of functional diaphragm innervation (Lenti-GFP: 2.58±0.26 mV, n=4 mice; Lenti-shRNA: 4.20±0.32 mV, n=4 mice; t-test, p=0.0075).
evidence: This claim is supported by CMAP recordings shown in Figure 3e-g.

claim: EphrinB2 knockdown had no impact on overall disease phenotype, including limb motor function, disease onset and progression, and animal survival.
source: As expected, given that injections were delivered only to levels C3-5, ephrinB2 knockdown in astrocytes had no impact on overall disease phenotype, including limb motor function, disease onset and progression, and animal survival, as assessed by a battery of established measurements (Lepore et al., 2008b; Lepore et al., 2011b; Lepore et al., 2010; Lepore et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple behavioral and survival measurements shown in Figure 4, including weight loss, grip strength, disease onset, and survival analyses.

claim: EphrinB2 knockdown did not affect weight loss at any age tested.
source: EphrinB2 knockdown did not affect weight loss at any age tested (F (1, 18)=0.17, p=0.69) (Figure 4a; n=8–10 mice per group).
evidence: This claim is supported by weight measurements shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Overall disease onset as determined by the timing of weight loss onset was unaffected by ephrinB2 knockdown.
source: Additionally, overall disease onset as determined by the timing of weight loss onset was unaffected, with both the lenti-GFP and lenti-shRNA groups showing similar onset as determined by Kaplan-Meier analysis (Lenti-GFP: 124.4 days; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2 123.5 days, chi square: 0.017, p=0.90, Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon test; n=8–9 mice per group) (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis of weight loss onset shown in Figure 4b.

claim: There were no differences between the two groups in either hindlimb or forelimb grip strength decline.
source: Furthermore, there were no differences between the two groups in either hindlimb (F (1, 18)=0.48, p=0.50, ANOVA; n=9–10 mice per group) (Figure 4c) or forelimb (F (1, 18)=0.95, p=0.34, ANOVA; n=9–10 mice per group) (Figure 4e) grip strength decline.
evidence: This claim is supported by grip strength measurements shown in Figure 4c and 4e.

claim: EphrinB2 knockdown had no effect on hindlimb disease onset.
source: EphrinB2 knockdown had no effect on either hindlimb disease onset (Lenti-GFP: 90.4 days; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2 103.0 days, chi square: 2.92, p=0.09, Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon test; n=9–10 mice per group) (Figure 4d) or forelimb disease onset (Lenti-GFP: 107.2 days; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2 105.1 days, chi square: 0.13, p=0.72, Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon test; n=9–10 mice per group) (Figure 4f).
evidence: This claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis of hindlimb disease onset shown in Figure 4d.

claim: EphrinB2 knockdown had no effect on forelimb disease onset.
source: EphrinB2 knockdown had no effect on either hindlimb disease onset (Lenti-GFP: 90.4 days; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2 103.0 days, chi square: 2.92, p=0.09, Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon test; n=9–10 mice per group) (Figure 4d) or forelimb disease onset (Lenti-GFP: 107.2 days; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2 105.1 days, chi square: 0.13, p=0.72, Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon test; n=9–10 mice per group) (Figure 4f).
evidence: This claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis of forelimb disease onset shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Compared to lenti-GFP control, lenti-shRNA had no effect on disease duration as measured by the time from weight onset to endstage.
source: Compared to lenti-GFP control, lenti-shRNA had no effect on disease duration as measured by the time from: weight onset to endstage (Lenti-GFP: 7.90±1.110 days, n=10 mice; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2: 11.38±1.963 days, p=0.13, unpaired t-test; n=8 mice) (Figure 4g); hindlimb disease onset to endstage (Lenti-GFP: 41.90±6.63 days, n=10 mice; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2: 29.44±6.34 days, n=9 mice, p=0.19, unpaired t-test) (Figure 4h); forelimb disease onset to endstage (Lenti-GFP: 25.10±6.48 days, n=10 mice; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2: 27.11±8.92 days, n=9 mice, p=0.86, unpaired t-test) (Figure 4i); or hindlimb disease onset to forelimb disease onset (Lenti-GFP: 16.80±4.14 days, n=10 mice; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2: 2.33±7.44 days, n=9 mice, p=0.099, unpaired t-test) (Figure 4j).
evidence: This claim is supported by disease duration measurements shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Compared to lenti-GFP control, lenti-shRNA had no effect on the age of disease endstage as determined by the righting reflex.
source: Compared to lenti-GFP control, lenti-shRNA had no effect on the age of disease endstage as determined by Kaplan-Meier analysis (Lenti-GFP: 132.3 days; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2 129.5 days, chi square: 0.24, p=0.63, Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon test; n=8–10 mice per group) (Figure 4k).
evidence: This claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 4k.

claim: The lenti-shRNA group showed a significant increase in the percentage of fully-innervated NMJs compared to control-treated animals.
source: Compared to control-treated animals (Figure 5d), the lenti-shRNA group (Figure 5e) showed a significant increase in the percentage of fully-innervated NMJs (Figure 5f) and a significant decrease in percentage of completely-denervated junctions (Figure 5g), demonstrating that lenti-shRNA treatment preserved PhMN innervation of the diaphragm (innervated: Lenti-GFP: 27.0 ± 2.5% of total NMJs, n=4 mice; Lenti-shRNA: 53.2±8.5, n=4; t-test, p=0.04) (denervated: Lenti-GFP: 21.6 ± 1.6% of total NMJs, n=4 mice; Lenti-shRNA: 8.0±3.7, n=4 mice; t-test, p=0.03).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMJ morphology analysis shown in Figure 5d-f.

claim: The lenti-shRNA group showed a significant decrease in percentage of completely-denervated NMJs compared to control-treated animals.
source: Compared to control-treated animals (Figure 5d), the lenti-shRNA group (Figure 5e) showed a significant increase in the percentage of fully-innervated NMJs (Figure 5f) and a significant decrease in percentage of completely-denervated junctions (Figure 5g), demonstrating that lenti-shRNA treatment preserved PhMN innervation of the diaphragm (innervated: Lenti-GFP: 27.0 ± 2.5% of total NMJs, n=4 mice; Lenti-shRNA: 53.2±8.5, n=4; t-test, p=0.04) (denervated: Lenti-GFP: 21.6 ± 1.6% of total NMJs, n=4 mice; Lenti-shRNA: 8.0±3.7, n=4 mice; t-test, p=0.03).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMJ morphology analysis shown in Figure 5d-e and 5g.

claim: In the lumbar enlargement, there was a large increase in ephrinB2 protein expression in the SOD1 mutation ALS samples compared to the non-diseased controls.
source: In the lumbar enlargement, there was a large increase in ephrinB2 protein expression in the SOD1 mutation ALS samples compared to the non-diseased controls (Figure 6) (non-ALS lumbar: 3.8±1.1 a.u.; ALS lumbar: 17.8±18.2; ALS cortex: 2.9±0.25; p=0.523, ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting analysis on postmortem human samples shown in Figure 6.

claim: Dramatic ephrinB2 upregulation in the SOD1 mutation samples was observed with only two of the three ALS donors.
source: There was some donor-to-donor variability; while all of the non-ALS control samples showed similarly lower levels of ephrinB2 protein expression in the lumbar spinal cord, dramatic ephrinB2 upregulation in the SOD1 mutation samples was observed with only two of the three ALS donors.
evidence: This claim is supported by the immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6 showing variability across ALS donors.

claim: GFAP protein levels were significantly higher in the two ALS samples with increased ephrinB2 expression.
source: To this point, we also performed GFAP immunoblotting on the same lumbar spinal cord samples and found signficantly higher GFAP protein levels in the two samples with increased ephrinB2 expression (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by GFAP immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6.

claim: EphrinB2 protein levels were not elevated in the frontal cortex of ALS donor samples.
source: Lastly, we did not observe increased ephrinB2 expression in a disease unaffected region in these same three ALS donor samples, as ephrinB2 protein levels were not elevated in frontal cortex (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting data from frontal cortex samples shown in Figure 6.

claim: EphrinB2 is expressed predominantly by ventral horn astrocytes in the SOD1G93A mouse model of ALS.
source: We have shown that ephrinB2 is expressed predominantly by ventral horn astrocytes and that ephrinB2 up-regulation coincided with progression of MN loss and overall disease phenotype in the SOD1G93A mouse model of ALS.
evidence: This claim is supported by the immunohistochemistry data showing co-localization of ephrinB2 with GFAP and the quantification of transduced cell types.

claim: EphrinB2 up-regulation coincided with progression of motor neuron loss and overall disease phenotype in the SOD1G93A mouse model of ALS.
source: We have shown that ephrinB2 is expressed predominantly by ventral horn astrocytes and that ephrinB2 up-regulation coincided with progression of MN loss and overall disease phenotype in the SOD1G93A mouse model of ALS.
evidence: This claim is supported by the temporal analysis of ephrinB2 expression at different disease stages (60 days, 120 days, endstage) shown in Figure 1.

claim: Reducing ephrinB2 expression in ventral horn astrocytes of the SOD1G93A mouse cervical spinal cord maintained diaphragmatic respiratory function by protecting cervical spinal cord motor neurons.
source: Furthermore, we found that reducing ephrinB2 expression in ventral horn astrocytes of the SOD1G93A mouse cervical spinal cord maintained diaphragmatic respiratory function by protecting cervical spinal cord MNs and preserving PhMN innervation of the diaphragm.
evidence: This claim is supported by the motor neuron counts, CMAP recordings, and NMJ morphology data shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Reducing ephrinB2 expression in ventral horn astrocytes of the SOD1G93A mouse cervical spinal cord maintained diaphragmatic respiratory function by preserving phrenic motor neuron innervation of the diaphragm.
source: Furthermore, we found that reducing ephrinB2 expression in ventral horn astrocytes of the SOD1G93A mouse cervical spinal cord maintained diaphragmatic respiratory function by protecting cervical spinal cord MNs and preserving PhMN innervation of the diaphragm.
evidence: This claim is supported by the CMAP recordings and NMJ morphology data shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Astrocyte ephrinB2 may play a non-cell autonomous role in ALS, in particular in mutant SOD1-associated disease.
source: Our findings suggest that astrocyte ephrinB2 may play a non-cell autonomous role in ALS, in particular in mutant SOD1-associated disease.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings showing that reducing ephrinB2 in astrocytes protects motor neurons.

claim: Astrocytes are involved in ALS pathogenesis via loss of critically important functions such as extracellular glutamate uptake.
source: A substantial body of work has demonstrated that astrocytes are involved in ALS pathogenesis (Ilieva et al., 2009; Yamanaka and Komine, 2018), both via loss of critically important functions such as extracellular glutamate uptake (Rothstein et al., 1995) and toxic gain-of-function such as altered transforming growth factor β (TGFβ) signaling (Phatnani et al., 2013) and increased production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Cassina et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on astrocyte dysfunction in ALS.

claim: Astrocytes are involved in ALS pathogenesis via toxic gain-of-function such as altered TGFβ signaling.
source: A substantial body of work has demonstrated that astrocytes are involved in ALS pathogenesis (Ilieva et al., 2009; Yamanaka and Komine, 2018), both via loss of critically important functions such as extracellular glutamate uptake (Rothstein et al., 1995) and toxic gain-of-function such as altered transforming growth factor β (TGFβ) signaling (Phatnani et al., 2013) and increased production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Cassina et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on TGFβ signaling in ALS astrocytes.

claim: Astrocytes are involved in ALS pathogenesis via toxic gain-of-function such as increased production of reactive oxygen species.
source: A substantial body of work has demonstrated that astrocytes are involved in ALS pathogenesis (Ilieva et al., 2009; Yamanaka and Komine, 2018), both via loss of critically important functions such as extracellular glutamate uptake (Rothstein et al., 1995) and toxic gain-of-function such as altered transforming growth factor β (TGFβ) signaling (Phatnani et al., 2013) and increased production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Cassina et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on ROS production by astrocytes in ALS.

claim: EphA4 receptor can be activated by ephrinA and ephrinB ligands including ephrinB2.
source: EphA4 receptor can be activated by ephrinA and ephrinB ligands including ephrinB2 (Flanagan and Vanderhaeghen, 1998), suggesting that astocyte ephrinB2 serves as a ligand mediating pathogenic actions in ALS.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on EphA4 receptor-ligand interactions.

claim: Astrocyte ephrinB2 serves as a ligand mediating pathogenic actions in ALS.
source: EphA4 receptor can be activated by ephrinA and ephrinB ligands including ephrinB2 (Flanagan and Vanderhaeghen, 1998), suggesting that astocyte ephrinB2 serves as a ligand mediating pathogenic actions in ALS.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the known receptor-ligand interactions and the experimental findings in the study.

claim: Genetic reduction of EphA4 in SOD1G93A mice did not impact disease measures.
source: Subsequent work in mouse models (Ling et al., 2018; Rué et al., 2019b; Zhao et al., 2018) showed that genetic reduction of EphA4 in SOD1G93A mice or intracerebroventricular delivery of an antisense oligonucleotide directed against EphA4 in both SOD1G93A and PFN1G118V mouse models of ALS did not impact disease measures.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on EphA4 genetic reduction studies in ALS models.

claim: Intracerebroventricular delivery of an antisense oligonucleotide directed against EphA4 in SOD1G93A and PFN1G118V mouse models of ALS did not impact disease measures.
source: Subsequent work in mouse models (Ling et al., 2018; Rué et al., 2019b; Zhao et al., 2018) showed that genetic reduction of EphA4 in SOD1G93A mice or intracerebroventricular delivery of an antisense oligonucleotide directed against EphA4 in both SOD1G93A and PFN1G118V mouse models of ALS did not impact disease measures.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on antisense oligonucleotide studies targeting EphA4 in ALS models.

claim: Administration of an EphA4 agonist to mutant SOD1 mouse increased both disease duration and animal survival.
source: In contrast, manipulations that target EphA4 signaling such as administration of an EphA4 agonist to mutant SOD1 mouse increased both disease duration and animal survival (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on EphA4 agonist treatment in ALS models.

claim: Delivery of soluble EphA4-Fc that blocks ligand binding to EphA4 results in partial preservation of motor function in SOD1G93A mice.
source: In addition, delivery of soluble EphA4-Fc that blocks ligand binding to EphA4 results in partial preservation of motor function in SOD1G93A mice (Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on EphA4-Fc treatment in ALS models.

claim: Genetic knockdown of ephrinA5 in the SOD1G93A mouse model accelerates disease progression and hastens animal death.
source: Supporting this notion, genetic knockdown of ephrinA5 (an EphA4 ligand) in the SOD1G93A mouse model accelerates disease progression and hastens animal death (Rué et al., 2019a), which may be explained by an enhancement of the EphA4-ephrinB2 interaction in the absence of ephrinA5.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on ephrinA5 knockdown in ALS models.

claim: The acceleration of disease progression following ephrinA5 knockdown may be explained by an enhancement of the EphA4-ephrinB2 interaction in the absence of ephrinA5.
source: Supporting this notion, genetic knockdown of ephrinA5 (an EphA4 ligand) in the SOD1G93A mouse model accelerates disease progression and hastens animal death (Rué et al., 2019a), which may be explained by an enhancement of the EphA4-ephrinB2 interaction in the absence of ephrinA5.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the mechanism underlying the ephrinA5 knockdown phenotype.

claim: Directly targeting ephrinB2 is a promising strategy to modulate both Eph-ephrin signaling and astrocyte-motor neuron interactions in ALS.
source: While other agents are also being developed to manipulate binding of ephrins with EphA4 for ALS therapeutics (Qin et al., 2015; Schoonaert et al., 2017), our results suggest that directly targeting ephrinB2 is a promising strategy to modulate both Eph-ephrin signaling and astrocyte-MN interactions in ALS.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing motor neuron protection and functional preservation following ephrinB2 knockdown.

claim: Unlike the effects of knocking down EphA4 expression in ALS animal models, significant motor neuron protection, maintenance of NMJ innervation and preservation of diaphragm muscle function was observed following ephrinB2 reduction.
source: Unlike the effects of knocking down EphA4 expression in ALS animal models, we observe significant MN protection, maintenance of NMJ innervation and preservation of diaphragm muscle function following ephrinB2 reduction.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the study showing these protective effects, in contrast to cited literature on EphA4 knockdown.

claim: Ephrin-B upregulation in chronic pain models results in increased NMDA receptor function and pathological synaptic plasticity via interaction with EphBs.
source: Consistent with this model, ephrin-B upregulation in chronic pain models results in increased NMDA receptor function and pathological synaptic plasticity via interaction with EphBs (Henderson and Dalva, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on ephrin-B signaling in chronic pain.

claim: EphBs are centrally involved in regulating subcellular localization of ionotropic glutamate receptor subunits to excitatory synapses.
source: EphB's are centrally involved in regulating subcellular localization of ionotropic glutamate receptor subunits to excitatory synapses (Hanamura et al., 2017; Nolt et al., 2011), raising the intriguing possibility that enhanced ephrinB2-EphB2 signaling results in increased glutamate receptor activation in MNs and consequently may be contributing to excitotoxicity that plays a well-known role in ALS.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on EphB function in glutamate receptor localization.

claim: Enhanced ephrinB2-EphB2 signaling may result in increased glutamate receptor activation in motor neurons and consequently may be contributing to excitotoxicity in ALS.
source: EphB's are centrally involved in regulating subcellular localization of ionotropic glutamate receptor subunits to excitatory synapses (Hanamura et al., 2017; Nolt et al., 2011), raising the intriguing possibility that enhanced ephrinB2-EphB2 signaling results in increased glutamate receptor activation in MNs and consequently may be contributing to excitotoxicity that plays a well-known role in ALS.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about a potential mechanism linking ephrinB2 upregulation to excitotoxicity in ALS.

claim: Single-nucleus RNAseq on mouse cervical spinal cord shows that alpha motor neurons of the cervical spinal cord express various EphA and EphB receptors.
source: Consistent with these studies, single-nucleus RNAseq on mouse cervical spinal cord shows that alpha MNs of the cervical spinal cord express various EphA and EphB receptors (http://spinalcordatlas.org/) (Alkaslasi et al., 2021; Blum et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published single-nucleus RNAseq data.

claim: Phrenic motor neurons express a number of EphA and EphB receptors, including EphA4.
source: In addition, this dataset identifies a PhMN-specific marker (ErbB4); by specifically looking at the expression profile of only the ErbB4-expressing cervical alpha MNs, the data reveal that PhMNs express a number of EphA's and EphB's, including EphA4.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of published single-nucleus RNAseq data and IHC validation mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: The effect of Efnb2-shRNA treatment was primarily due to changes in astrocytes.
source: However, we observed (1) dramatic ephrinB2 upregulation in the ventral horn of SOD1G93A mice that appears to be astrocyte-specific, (2) transduction predominately of astrocytes with our vector, and (3) significant reduction of ephrinB2 expression almost entirely in astrocytes in shRNA-treated animals. These data suggest that the effect of Efnb2-shRNA treatment was primarily due to changes in astrocytes and that astrocyte expression is the likely mechanism underlying ephrinB2's action in mutant SOD1-associated ALS.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple lines of experimental evidence showing astrocyte-specific ephrinB2 upregulation and knockdown.

claim: Astrocyte expression is the likely mechanism underlying ephrinB2's action in mutant SOD1-associated ALS.
source: However, we observed (1) dramatic ephrinB2 upregulation in the ventral horn of SOD1G93A mice that appears to be astrocyte-specific, (2) transduction predominately of astrocytes with our vector, and (3) significant reduction of ephrinB2 expression almost entirely in astrocytes in shRNA-treated animals. These data suggest that the effect of Efnb2-shRNA treatment was primarily due to changes in astrocytes and that astrocyte expression is the likely mechanism underlying ephrinB2's action in mutant SOD1-associated ALS.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings showing astrocyte-specific effects.

claim: There is a modest increase in astrocyte number in ventral horn of the SOD1G93A mouse model at time points following phenotypic disease onset.
source: We previously showed that there is a modest increase in astrocyte number in ventral horn of the SOD1G93A mouse model at time points following phenotypic disease onset (Lepore et al., 2008a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The total increase in ephrinB2 expression across the ventral horn was not due to just the small increase in astrocyte numbers but was instead due to the dramatically elevated ephrinB2 expression observed across the astrocyte population.
source: Throughout disease course in these SOD1G93A mice, ephrinB2 level in individual astrocytes dramatically increases (including across most or all astrocytes), suggesting that the total increase in ephrinB2 expression across the ventral horn was not due to just this small increase in astrocyte numbers but was instead due to the dramatically elevated ephrinB2 expression observed across the astrocyte population.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that ephrinB2 levels increase dramatically in individual astrocytes.

claim: ALS is heterogeneous both with respect to its genetic basis and its clinical disease course.
source: ALS is heterogeneous both with respect to its genetic basis and its clinical disease course (e.g. age and site of onset; severity/progression; Mitsumoto et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on ALS heterogeneity and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Patients with mutations in the same gene show variability in their clinical disease manifestation such as the rate of disease progression depending on the specific SOD1 mutation.
source: Furthermore, these familial cases are associated with mutations in a number of different genes. In addition, patients (even with mutations in the same gene) show variability in their clinical disease manifestation such as the rate of disease progression depending on, for example, the specific SOD1 mutation (Andersen et al., 1997; Radunovíc and Leigh, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on genotype-phenotype correlations in ALS.

claim: Respiratory function involves the contribution of a number of other muscle groups besides diaphragm, and these muscles are innervated by various lower motor neuron pools located across a relatively-large expanse of the CNS neuraxis.
source: Respiratory function involves the contribution of a number of other muscle groups besides diaphragm, and these muscles are innervated by various lower MN pools located across a relatively-large expanse of the CNS neuraxis.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of respiratory neuroanatomy.

claim: CMAP recording is a powerful assay of functional innervation of diaphragm muscle by phrenic motor axons.
source: While CMAP recording is a powerful assay of functional innervation of diaphragm muscle by phrenic motor axons, it does not directly measure overall respiratory function.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of electrophysiological techniques.

claim: The forelimb grip strength assay is impacted primarily by distal forelimb muscle groups controlled by motor neuron pools located at more caudal locations of the spinal cord (i.e. low cervical and high thoracic).
source: However, this grip strength motor assay is impacted primarily by distal forelimb muscle groups controlled by MN pools located at more caudal locations of the spinal cord (i.e. low cervical and high thoracic), likely explaining the lack of effect on grip strength.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of motor control neuroanatomy and inference about why grip strength was not affected.

claim: Astrocyte ephrinB2 upregulation is both a signaling mechanism underlying astrocyte pathogenicity in mutant SOD1-associated ALS and a promising therapeutic target.
source: In conclusion, our findings suggest that astrocyte ephrinB2 upregulation is both a signaling mechanism underlying astrocyte pathogenicity in mutant SOD1-associated ALS and a promising therapeutic target.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings showing ephrinB2 upregulation in disease and protective effects of knockdown.

claim: All diaphragm NMJs in non-diseased WT mice are completely intact.
source: Although we assessed NMJ morphology only in SOD1G93A mice in this work, our previous findings show that all diaphragm NMJs in non-diseased WT mice are completely intact (Nicaise et al., 2012b; Lepore et al., 2010; Li et al., 2015b; Martin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: There is extensive denervation at a large portion of NMJs across the diaphragm at 117 days of age in SOD1G93A mice.
source: In the current study, we find extensive denervation at a large portion of NMJs across the diaphragm at 117 days of age in SOD1G93A mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by the NMJ morphology data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The increased cervical motor neuron survival in the lenti-shRNA-Efnb2 group coincided with enhanced preservation of diaphragm NMJ innervation.
source: The increased cervical MN survival in the lenti-shRNA-Efnb2 group coincided with enhanced preservation of diaphragm NMJ innervation, suggesting that the ephrinB2 knockdown-mediated effects on NMJ innervation and CMAP amplitudes were due at least in part to protection of PhMNs centrally within the cervical spinal cord.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the correlation between motor neuron survival and NMJ preservation.

claim: The ephrinB2 knockdown-mediated effects on NMJ innervation and CMAP amplitudes were due at least in part to protection of phrenic motor neurons centrally within the cervical spinal cord.
source: The increased cervical MN survival in the lenti-shRNA-Efnb2 group coincided with enhanced preservation of diaphragm NMJ innervation, suggesting that the ephrinB2 knockdown-mediated effects on NMJ innervation and CMAP amplitudes were due at least in part to protection of PhMNs centrally within the cervical spinal cord.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the correlation between central motor neuron protection and peripheral functional preservation.

claim: The absence of ephrinB2 upregulation in one ALS sample may be related to the anatomical progression of disease in this particular donor.
source: The absence of ephrinB2 upregulation in the one ALS sample may be related to the anatomical progression of disease in this particular donor.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about why one ALS donor did not show ephrinB2 upregulation.

claim: The level of GFAP expression is often used as an indicator of disease progression at a particular anatomical region.
source: As the level of GFAP expression is often used as an indicator of disease progression at a particular anatomical region, this finding suggests that ephrinB2 upregulation may have occurred selectively at locations in the CNS where disease processes were already occurring by the time of death.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about GFAP as a marker of astrocyte reactivity and disease progression.

claim: EphrinB2 upregulation may have occurred selectively at locations in the CNS where disease processes were already occurring by the time of death.
source: As the level of GFAP expression is often used as an indicator of disease progression at a particular anatomical region, this finding suggests that ephrinB2 upregulation may have occurred selectively at locations in the CNS where disease processes were already occurring by the time of death.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the correlation between GFAP and ephrinB2 expression in the human samples.

claim: Focal protection of cervical enlargement motor neurons using glial progenitor transplantation extends overall disease phenotype in SOD1G93A rodents.
source: That being said, PhMN preservation plays a critical role in both SOD1G93A models and human disease (Lladó et al., 2006), and we have previously shown that focal protection of cervical enlargement MNs using glial progenitor transplantation does extend overall disease phenotype in SOD1G93A rodents (Lepore et al., 2008b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Phrenic motor neuron preservation plays a critical role in both SOD1G93A models and human disease.
source: That being said, PhMN preservation plays a critical role in both SOD1G93A models and human disease (Lladó et al., 2006), and we have previously shown that focal protection of cervical enlargement MNs using glial progenitor transplantation does extend overall disease phenotype in SOD1G93A rodents (Lepore et al., 2008b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on phrenic motor neuron importance in ALS.
